sections.title: Unusual Kiddushei Kesef: *Arev*, Canaanite Slave, Important Man
sections.gist: Three cases where the money doesn't pass from husband to wife (*arev*, Canaanite slave, both combined), Rava's question about a woman who pays the man, and why the mechanisms had to be taught for monetary acquisitions too.

children.title: Rava's Three Cases: *Arev*, Canaanite Slave, or Both
children.gist: Money goes to a third party, comes from a third party, or both, and Rava validates each case with the law of an *arev* (guarantor), of a freed slave, or of the two together.

bullets.text: To follow the cases, keep three parties in view: the woman, the man who pays or marries, and "so-and-so", a third party. In each case the usual path of *kiddushei kesef*, money from husband to wife, is broken.

children.title: *Arev*: She Commits Herself Without Benefit
children.gist: A woman who has the man pay a third party is betrothed to him, just as an *arev* binds himself though the loan goes to someone else.

bullets.text: Rava: a woman says, "Give 100 dinars to so-and-so, and I will be betrothed to you." She is betrothed, by the law of a guarantor (*arev*).
An *arev* commits himself to repay even though the loan goes to the borrower and he gets nothing. So too she commits and transfers herself to the man who paid, though the money went to someone else.
The case strains the basic idea of *kiddushei kesef*: the woman receives nothing, yet the money effects her betrothal. The rishonim divide over how it works.

Rashi: *arev*, slave and the combined case are recognized transactional forms, and what works in them works for kiddushin. Later rishonim find this hard, and Rashi and others add that the link to kiddushin must be stated explicitly.
Rosh: what matters is that a formal transfer of money took place, whatever its direction. Kiddushin attaches to that event rather than to a purchase of the woman.

Rambam: she gains a psychological benefit, worth a peruta, from the man acting on her financial request. The same idea returns later in the tractate ("dance for me and be betrothed"), though the Gemara says nothing of it here.
Ritva takes a middle path: partly the transfer of money, partly the psychological benefit. Whose money goes to the third party, hers or his, is itself disputed.

children.title: Canaanite Slave: He Acquires Without Losing
children.gist: A man gives the woman money for her betrothal to a third party, who acquires her without paying, just as a slave is freed by another's money.

bullets.text: A man gives a woman 100 dinars: "Here are 100; with them become betrothed to so-and-so." She is betrothed to so-and-so, by the law of freeing a Canaanite slave.
A Canaanite slave acquires himself when another person pays his master, though he loses nothing of his own. So too so-and-so acquires her with another man's money.

A slave can't free himself with his own money, which already belongs to his master; a third party must pay, yet it is the slave's status that changes. Kiddushin likewise is a change of status, not a purchase.

children.title: Both Together: Each Analogy Covers the Other's Gap
children.gist: When the woman gets nothing and the husband pays nothing, neither the *arev* nor the slave alone suffices, but together they validate the betrothal.

bullets.text: A woman says: "Give 100 dinars to so-and-so and I will be betrothed to him." She is betrothed, from the two laws combined.

The *arev* explains her committing herself without benefit. But in the *arev* case the one who acquires (the lender) is the one who pays, while here so-and-so pays nothing. The freed slave shows one can acquire without paying.

But in the slave case the master who transfers ownership receives the money, while here she transfers herself and receives nothing. The *arev* shows one can commit oneself without benefit. Together they cover the case.

children.title: Woman Pays the Man: Kinyan Agav or Adam Chashuv?
children.gist: Rava asks about a woman who gives the man money; Rav Ashi objects that land-like property can't come along with movables, and Mar Zutra answers that an important man's accepting her gift is itself her benefit.

bullets.text: Rava's question: a woman says to a man, "Here are 100 dinars, and I will be betrothed to you." Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa: she is betrothed.
Rav Ashi objects: then property that serves as a guarantee (land, and a person likewise) is acquired by acquiring property that does not (money).
But the Mishnah (26a) teaches the reverse: unguaranteed property is acquired along with guaranteed property, through money, document or taking possession, and not the other way around.
This is the rule of *kinyan agav*: movables ride along with land, never land with movables. It is like buying a flock and claiming the field comes with it.
Mar Zutra: no acquiring-along-with is involved. The case is an important man (*adam chashuv*): for the benefit of having him accept a gift from her, she agrees to give herself to him.

Rashi: an important man refuses gifts on principle ("*sonei matanot yichyeh*"). When he accepts hers, the benefit to her is real and worth a peruta, like a dignitary who never accepts hospitality letting you pay for his dinner.

Here the Gemara states outright the kind of psychological benefit the Rambam reads into the *arev* case. In practice it is narrow, limited to a man known to refuse gifts, so a woman does not betroth a man with a ring.
Is a free person really comparable to land? Rashi seems to say so; Tosafot limit the comparison to Canaanite slaves, whom a verse likens to land. The Shach brings many proofs against Tosafot.

children.title: Monetary Matters Too: Eager Brides vs. Waivable Claims
children.gist: Rava applies the *arev* and slave mechanisms to ordinary acquisitions as well, and the Gemara explains why neither kiddushin nor monetary law could be learned from the other.

bullets.text: Returning to the *arev* and slave cases: it was also stated in Rava's name that the same modes of acquisition work in monetary matters, and both statements are needed.

From kiddushin alone one might limit it: a woman agrees to betrothal for any benefit, as Reish Lakish cites the saying among women, *tav le'meitav tan du mi'le'meitav armelu*, better to sit as two than to sit alone like a widow.
From monetary matters alone one might limit it: a monetary claim can be waived without receiving anything. Betrothal doesn't rest on her will alone, since she must actually receive money.
A man and woman who simply agree to marry, with no kinyan, are not betrothed. Since the formal act is constitutive, a gap in it can't be smoothed over by *mechilah* as it can in money matters.

A buyer or seller has no such eagerness

sections.title: Half-Betrothal: Half of Me, Half of You, and Spreading
sections.gist: Rava's distinction between "half of me" and "half of you", Mar Zutra son of Rav Mari's challenge that the betrothal should spread like consecration, and R. Yochanan's partners' animal with its three lessons on *dichui*.

children.title: "Half of Me" vs. "Half of You": One Husband, Two Wives
children.gist: A man may betroth a woman to half of himself, since he may take a second wife, but not half of her, since she can't have two husbands.

bullets.text: Rava: "Be betrothed to half of me": she is betrothed. "Half of you is betrothed to me": she is not betrothed.
Abaye: if the reason is "When a man takes a woman" (Devarim 24:1), a whole woman and not half, the verse also says "a man", not half a man.
Rava: the cases differ. A woman is not eligible for two men, so betrothing half of her leaves the other half for someone else, which is impossible.
A man may marry two women. "Half of me" means: if I wish to marry another woman, I will.
Rava answers from reasoning, not from the verse. The case implies a man can reserve at the outset his right to a second wife; the Gemara doesn't ask whether he must.

illustration.caption: Rava's distinction (7a): "half of me" leaves room for a second wife, which is possible, while "half of you" would leave room for a second husband, which is not.

children.title: Should It Spread Like Consecration? An Animal vs. Another Mind
children.gist: Consecrating an animal's leg sanctifies the whole animal, so why shouldn't "half of you" spread to all of her? Because the woman has a mind of her own, and the betrothal depends on her consent.

bullets.text: Mar Zutra son of Rav Mari to Ravina: let the betrothal of "half of you" spread through all of her. A baraita (Tosefta Temurah 1:5): "The leg of this animal is an *olah*" makes the whole animal an *olah*.

Even the view that the whole isn't an *olah* speaks of a leg, which the animal can live without. Consecrating a part its life depends on makes all of it an *olah*, and a woman can't live without half her body.
Rejected: the animal has no mind, but here there is another mind (*da'at acheret*), the woman's, and she must agree for the betrothal to take effect.
Her acceptance is acceptance of the words offered to her. If he said "half of you", that is all she agreed to, and the betrothal can't reach beyond her consent.

children.title: R. Yochanan's Partners' Animal: Three Lessons in Dichui
children.gist: The case compares to an animal consecrated half by half: it becomes holy and can make a substitute, but may never be offered, and from it the Gemara learns three rules of permanent *dichui* (deferral).

bullets.text: The true parallel is R. Yochanan's case: an animal of two partners; one consecrates his half, then buys the other half and consecrates it. It is consecrated but may not be offered, since it was unfit when first consecrated.
The consecration didn't spread to the whole animal without the partner's consent, just as the betrothal doesn't spread without the woman's.
Being consecrated, it makes a non-sacred animal exchanged for it a substitute (*temurah*). The substitute is like it: consecrated, but not offered.
On the shiur's reading, *temurah* requires sanctity of the body itself, so the half-and-half animal has that level of sanctity even though it can't be offered.

Three lessons: living animals can be permanently deferred (*dichui*); a disqualification present from the outset counts as *dichui*; and *dichui* applies even to consecration of value (*kedushat damim*).

sections.title: One Peruta, Split Several Ways: Unresolved Questions
sections.gist: A run of questions left as *teiku*: halves of one woman with halves of a peruta, two daughters for two sons with one peruta, and a daughter bought together with a cow or with land.

bullets.text: Most rishonim, the Rambam among them, rule stringently when a question of kiddushin is left unresolved.

children.title: Rava's Ladder: Split Statements or Counting Toward One?
children.gist: Four formulations, each asked only if the one before is joined: half-perutot, whole perutot, today and tomorrow, and "your two halves" with one peruta.

bullets.text: Rava: "Half of you with half a peruta, and half of you with half a peruta." Did saying "half a peruta" divide the act (and half a peruta can't betroth), or was he counting toward the whole sum at once?
If that counts as counting: "Half of you with a peruta, and half with a peruta." Did naming a full peruta for each half divide it, or does whatever he does that day count as counting?
If the whole day counts: "Half of you with a peruta today, and half with a peruta tomorrow." Does "tomorrow" divide it, or does he mean the betrothal begins now and is completed tomorrow?
The step from hours to a whole day is notable: the question is framed in days, not in the minutes that usually separate one act from another.
And: "Your two halves with one peruta." Here he spoke all at once; or can a woman not be betrothed in halves at all? None of these is resolved: *teiku*.
Framing kiddushin in halves, even halves that add up in one breath, may reflect a flawed idea of marriage, or offer the woman something she can't meaningfully accept.

chart.caption: Rava's four formulations: why each might be split or joined
rows: Half with half a peruta, half with half a peruta

A full peruta for each half makes two acts

Half with a peruta today, half tomorrow
The betrothal begins now and is completed tomorrow
Your two halves with one peruta
A woman can't be betrothed in halves at all

children.title: Two Daughters to Two Sons: Follow the Transactors or the Couples?
children.gist: One peruta passes between two fathers for two betrothals: is that money, or does each couple lack its peruta?

bullets.text: Rava: one man says to another, "Let your two daughters be betrothed to my two sons with one peruta."
Do we follow the giver and recipient, between whom a full peruta passes, or the sons and daughters, none of whom has a peruta of his own? *Teiku*.
The father must be acting as his sons' agent, since he can't betroth a wife for his son without the son's authorization.

children.title: Daughter with Cow or Land: Half a Peruta Each, or Separate Acquisitions?
children.gist: A daughter and an animal, or a daughter and a field, acquired together "with one peruta": is the peruta halved, or does the daughter get it all while the cow is pulled and the land possessed?

bullets.text: Rav Pappa: "I acquire your daughter and your cow with one peruta." Half a peruta each, so neither takes effect? Or the whole peruta for the daughter and the cow acquired by pulling (*meshikhah*)? *Teiku*.
Rav Ashi: "your daughter and your land with one peruta." Half a peruta each, or the peruta for the daughter and the land by taking possession (*chazakah*)? *Teiku*.
The land case has its own texture, since a person was compared to land in Rav Ashi's objection about a woman who pays the man.

sections.title: Silk Kiddushin: Must the Value Be Appraised (Shuma)?
sections.gist: Rabba and Rav Yosef on whether silk given for kiddushin must first be appraised; in a second version the dispute rests on Rav Yosef's rule that *shaveh kesef* needs a set value, which he proves from the Hebrew slave.

chart.caption: Silk given for kiddushin: when is appraisal (*shuma*) needed?
rows: *Shuma* needed: she isn't an expert and doesn't rely on him
*Shuma* needed: an item used as money must have a set value

children.title: Rabba vs. Rav Yosef: Agreed Cases and the Dispute
children.gist: All agree when he says "whatever it's worth" and when he overstated the value; they differ when his stated value is correct but she can't judge it.

bullets.text: A man betrothed a woman with silk. Rabba: no *shuma* (appraisal) is needed, since it is surely worth a peruta. Rav Yosef: *shuma* is needed.
All agree: if he said "be betrothed with them, whatever they're worth", no *shuma* is needed. If he said they're worth 50 dinars and they aren't, she is not betrothed.
The dispute: he said 50 and they are worth 50. Rabba: no *shuma* needed. Rav Yosef: needed, since she is no expert, doesn't rely on his estimate, and so doesn't truly agree.
Silk was reaching Babylonia from China in just this period: new, costly and hard to value. The dispute stands behind the practice of betrothing with a plain metal ring whose value is easy to know.

children.title: Another Version: Shaveh Kesef Needs a Set Value Like Money
children.gist: In a second version they disagree even over "whatever it's worth", because Rav Yosef holds that property given as money must have a fixed value like money.

bullets.text: Some say (*ika de'amrei*): they disagree even when he said "be betrothed with these, whatever they're worth."
Rav Yosef: *shaveh kesef* is like money in every way. Money has a set value (*kayitz*), so an item used as money must have a set value too.
On this version the concern isn't only her consent: silk, whose price varies and needs an expert, simply lacks money's defining quality unless it is appraised.

children.title: Rav Yosef's Source: A Hebrew Slave Isn't Redeemed with Grain or Vessels
children.gist: A baraita excludes grain and vessels from redeeming a Hebrew slave, and Rav Yosef shows this can only mean items worth a peruta but lacking a set value.

bullets.text: A baraita on the Hebrew slave: "out of the money that he was bought for" (Vayikra 25:51) means he is acquired with money, not with grain or vessels.
It can't mean items of value are excluded altogether: "he shall give back the price of his redemption" includes anything worth money.
Nor items worth less than a peruta, for then why name grain and vessels, when even coins under a peruta fail?
So they are worth a peruta but lack a set value. Redemption needs money or an item of clearly defined value, like money.

The Rama (siman 695) says not to send *mishloach manot* to a widow, for fear of a doubtful betrothal. The acharonim are puzzled, since both parties' intent is needed; the broad mechanisms of this daf, such as psychological benefit and the important man, may explain the concern.

key_terms.sense: betrothal through money or its value
key_terms.definition: Betrothal effected when the man gives the woman money or an item worth at least a peruta for the purpose of betrothal, with her consent.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rava stretches the mechanism to cases where the money goes to a third party, comes from a third party, or passes from the woman to the man.

key_terms.sense: a guarantor who binds himself without benefit
key_terms.definition: A guarantor on a loan, who obligates himself to repay if the borrower defaults even though the loan money goes to the borrower and not to him.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rava learns from the guarantor that a woman can bind herself in betrothal when the money is paid to someone else.

key_terms.definition: Movable property (without guarantee) can be acquired together with land (property that serves as a guarantee) through the act that acquires the land; the reverse, land acquired along with movables, does not work.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Ashi objects that a woman paying the man would make the woman, likened to land, come along with the money, the reverse of the rule.

key_terms.sense: an important man whose acceptance confers benefit
key_terms.definition: A person of standing whose acceptance of a gift or favor is itself a tangible benefit to the giver, which can serve as the value in a transaction.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Mar Zutra validates a woman's betrothing herself by paying the man only where he is an important man, whose accepting her gift is her benefit.

key_terms.definition: The rule that a consecrated animal disqualified from the altar may remain permanently barred from being offered, even if the disqualifying condition later passes.
key_terms.on_this_daf: From R. Yochanan's partners' animal the Gemara learns that deferral applies to living animals, to a disqualification present from the outset, and to consecration of value.

key_terms.sense: property given in place of money
key_terms.definition: An item worth money, which can generally be used wherever the Torah requires payment in money, as long as it has the required value.
key_terms.on_this_daf: In the second version, Rav Yosef holds that such an item must have a set value like money, as shown by the redemption of a Hebrew slave.

key_terms.definition: An assessment of the market value of an item used in a transaction, establishing that it is worth what is claimed.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rabba and Rav Yosef dispute whether silk given for kiddushin must be appraised when the stated value is correct but the woman can't judge it.

judgment_calls: Rava's question about a woman who pays the man (7a.6–7) and the extension to monetary matters (7a.8–10) are kept as children of one parent with the three cases, since all are unusual mechanisms of kiddushei kesef; the woman-pays case could stand as its own top-level section. The monetary extension stays where it falls, with a returns_to link to the three cases (the Gemara itself says it 'reverts back').

R. Yochanan's partners' animal and the three lessons on dichui are kept under half-betrothal, since the Gemara brings the case as the true parallel to 'half of you'; the three lessons are conceptually a hekdesh digression and could be a separate top-level section.
The three cases are split into three children with a chart on the parent, rather than one flat section, because each has its own analogy and the combined case has its own two-step argument.

The four unresolved questions are grouped under one parent, with Rava's four-step ladder as a single child (the steps are one chain); the two-daughters and daughter-plus-property questions could each be top-level.
The silk chart sits on the parent section because it spans both versions of the dispute (s17 and s18).
coverage_notes: The Sefaria text supplied ends at 8a.4, but the scope runs to 8a.9. The last section is anchored to 8a.9 as instructed, but its content is outlined only through 8a.4; lines 8a.5–8a.9 should be checked and filled in.
The essay attributes the two-daughters question to Rav Pappa; the text has Rava raising it. Followed the text.
The essay attributes the daughter-and-cow question to Rav Ashi; the text has Rav Pappa (Rav Ashi asks the daughter-and-land question). Followed the text.
The segmentation and essay spell the disputant 'Raba'; the text has Rabba. Followed the text.

The essay has Rava tell Abaye not to cite verses at him; the text only has Rava say 'How can these cases be compared?' before giving his reason. Kept the text's wording; the characterization appears only as shiur framing.
The essay presents the second rung of Rava's ladder as the same counting principle; the text's side is that whatever he does that day counts as counting. Followed the text.

The Rashi/Rosh/Rambam/Ritva analysis of the guarantor case, the Rashi/Tosafot/Shach debate on comparing persons to land, the historical note on silk and the Rama on mishloach manot are shiur material, marked as such.
The previous daf's essay tail covers the conditional-gift sugya ending at 6b.14, outside this scope; nothing from it was needed.
